Article Title: Centre tells SC it is open to tougher labels on packaged foods high in sugar, salt or fat
Article Text:
Supreme Court Justice JB Pardiwala questioned why the FSSAI was taking a two-phased approach.

NIN flags gaps in proposed system

Why the labels matter

NEW DELHI: The Centre on Thursday told the Supreme Court that it was willing to consider stronger warning labels on packaged food, opening the door to tighter front-of-pack labelling rules that could have a significant impact on the country's packaged food industry.The issue concerns a proposed system under which food packets would carry prominent red hexagonal warnings to alert consumers when products contain high levels of nutrients linked to health risks, reported news agency Reuters.The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) had recently proposed introducing the labelling system in two phases. Under the initial plan, a product would get a red warning symbol if it crossed the prescribed limits in at least two of three categories, namely added sugar, salt or saturated fat. Tighter provisions were to follow in the second phase.Health experts and activists have opposed this approach, arguing that requiring a product to be high in two nutrients before triggering a warning could allow several unhealthy products to avoid the label.The Supreme Court questioned the need for such a phased approach during Thursday's hearing."It has to be sugar ‌and salt. Only then will you ask them to put a label?" Justice JB Pardiwala asked the government's lawyer, stressing the word "and".Additional Solicitor General Brijender Chahar, appearing for FSSAI, said the regulator could now consider implementing both phases together following the court's observation.That could mean a product would carry a red warning if it crosses the limit for even one of the specified nutrients, whether added sugar, salt or saturated fat.The matter has been under the Supreme Court's consideration for months following petitions seeking stronger front-of-pack nutrition warnings. The court had recently given FSSAI a two-week deadline to come back with its proposals.As that deadline approached, the National Institute of Nutrition in Hyderabad submitted its suggestions to the food regulator.NIN has argued that the proposed system should not focus only on added sugar and added fat. It has suggested that factors such as total calories, total sugar and total fat should also be taken into account when deciding whether a packaged food needs a warning.The concern is that looking at only selected nutrients could allow some foods with an unhealthy overall nutritional profile to escape the warning system.A scientist from NIN explained this using fried snacks as an example. A packet of salty fried chips may contain little added sugar and could fall below the proposed threshold for added fat, while still being extremely calorie-dense because of its fat content.Under a system focused only on added sugar and added fat, such a product could therefore avoid a red warning despite being unhealthy when consumed frequently.Front-of-pack nutrition labelling is intended to give consumers an easy-to-understand warning without requiring them to study detailed nutritional information printed on the back of a packet.The proposed red hexagon is designed to work much like a stop sign, with words such as "high fat", "high sugar" or "high salt" clearly displayed depending on which limit a product crosses.NIN has also pointed out that the nutritional quality of a food cannot necessarily be determined simply by whether it is ultra-processed. A samosa or jalebi, for instance, may be high in fat or sugar without being classified as an ultra-processed food. At the same time, some whole-grain breakfast cereals may be ultra-processed but relatively low in fat, salt and sugar.The debate before the court is therefore not merely about the shape or colour of a label. It is about what nutritional criteria should trigger a warning and whether the proposed system is strong enough to help consumers identify foods that could be harmful when eaten regularly.
Article Summary: Centre willing to consider stronger warning labels on packaged food. Issue concerns a proposed system under which food packets would carry prominent red hexagonal warnings. Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) had proposed introducing the labelling system in two phases. Under the initial plan, a product would get a red warning symbol if it crossed the prescribed limits in at least two of three categories.

Article Title: AI making it difficult for central banks to determine growth potential: BIS
Article Text:
AI is making it harder for central banks to determine an economy’s potential growth rate.

Mumbai:

AI is making it harder for central banks to determine an economy’s potential growth rate, as technological change increases uncertainty around productivity, potential output and the natural rate of interest, BIS general manager Pablo Hernández de Cos said.“AI is reshaping demand, supply and financial markets simultaneously, making the economy harder to read and increasing uncertainty around the transmission of monetary policy,” Hernández de Cos said at the Global Fintech Fest in Mumbai on Thursday.While the objectives of monetary policy remain unchanged, AI-driven structural changes could make some of the key variables that guide policy harder to estimate, he said. Potential output and the natural rate of interest are already subject to significant uncertainty, and rapid changes driven by AI could widen measurement errors and increase discrepancies between actual and estimated output gaps.The longer-term economic impact of AI is also uncertain, Hernández de Cos said, pointing to three scenarios outlined in the BIS Annual Economic Report. In one, AI produces a bounded productivity boost that permanently raises the growth trend.In another, AI generates self-reinforcing, transformative growth as the technology improves itself. A third scenario, the “demand bottleneck”, sees automation diverting income from labour towards further AI investment, eventually weakening consumer spending and causing productivity and output growth to stall.These scenarios could have very different implications for the natural rate of interest and inflation, he said. Stronger productivity growth could raise r-star, while a demand bottleneck could eventually push it below pre-AI levels and become disinflationary.“The takeaway from this analysis is that there is considerable uncertainty about the long-term effects of AI,” Hernández de Cos said. The eventual outcome would depend on how much AI progress relies on consumer demand, how competition affects profit margins in the AI sector and how quickly AI products and infrastructure depreciate.Hernández de Cos flagged financial-stability risks from the AI investment boom, with concentrated equity valuations, capex outpacing cash flows and rising reliance on debt/private credit. Opaque “circular financing” between chipmakers, hyperscalers and AI firms could amplify losses if AI returns disappoint, turning the investment boom into a bust.AI could also deliver major productivity gains, with studies showing 10-65% task-level gains and 20-50% time savings; median estimates suggest a 0.5 percentage-point annual boost to total factor productivity. But benefits will be uneven: AI may augment skilled work while displacing routine cognitive jobs, with informal workers in developing economies particularly vulnerable. Early displacement is emerging in customer support, programming and administration, making reskilling essential.Advanced economies are better placed to capture near-term gains, though preparedness varies sharply among emerging markets. India has an opportunity to close the gap by building on its digital public infrastructure. Rather than replicate full AI ecosystems, countries should target comparative advantages across chips, cloud, data, models and applications, including local-language models and domain-specific data.For central banks, AI raises the premium on measurement, judgement, policy agility and international cooperation. Its economic impact will ultimately depend on policy choices, including investment in digital infrastructure and skills, competition, data governance and sound institutions.
Article Summary: AI is making it harder for central banks to determine an economy’s potential growth rate. technological change increases uncertainty around productivity, potential output and the natural rate of interest, BIS general manager Pablo Hernández de Cos said.

Article Title: Brics summit: 3 Russian aircraft touch down at Noida airport ahead of Putin's meet with PM Modi
Article Text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin’s three-day India visit will focus on defence, energy and economic ties, Ukraine and West Asia, with talks with PM Modi and participation in the BRICS summit on the agenda. (File photo)

NEW DELHI: Three Russian transport aircraft touched down at Noida International Airport on Thursday as world leaders began arriving in India ahead of the 18th BRICS Summit. The aircraft arrivals come a day ahead of Russian President Vladimir Putin's expected visit to New Delhi for the summit.Putin is also likely to hold a bilateral meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday, September 11, before the multilateral event scheduled to be held in New Delhi on September 12 and 13.Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov had earlier confirmed that the meeting between Putin and PM Modi was scheduled for Friday. Speaking to reporters during a virtual briefing from Moscow, Peskov said, "We're looking forward to the President and Prime Minister having another bilateral meeting during the visit. It is scheduled. It is scheduled for Friday, so first, like always, they will touch on the bilateral agenda. Trade and economic cooperation is a very wide scope."Peskov said Putin's India visit would provide an opportunity for the two sides to discuss bilateral relations and expand cooperation. He also expressed hope that India would successfully host the Brics summit."In a couple of days, President Putin will begin his India visit.You know that our two leaders, Indian and Russian leaders, are in a very close personal contact. They are very pragmatic in their relationship, and they are as sincere as to be able to discuss in a very open and constructive way the most sensitive issues of our agenda and our bilateral relations. Of course, it opens additional horizons for our cooperation," Peskov said.On the Brics summit, he said Russia was working to support greater cooperation among member countries across key areas."We have no doubt that the summit will be successful. Russia, we are doing our best to contribute to further development of BRICS cooperation in the three main pillars of our interaction. So, those are policy and security, economy and finance, and cultural and humanitarian contexts. So, we are supporting the idea of inviting new countries to join different formats within BRICS," he noted.India is hosting the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12 and 13, 2026. The summit is being held under the theme, “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.”
Article Summary: Three Russian transport aircraft touched down at Noida International Airport on Thursday as world leaders began arriving in India. The aircraft arrivals come a day ahead of Russian President Vladimir Putin's expected visit to New Delhi for the summit. Putin is also likely to hold a bilateral meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday.

Article Title: SC rejects 1993 blast accused Abu Salem's plea for early release from life term
Article Text:
Salem was extradited from Portugal on November 11, 2005, after a prolonged legal battle.

The Supreme Court dismissed a plea by gangster Abu Salem on Thursday after he sought an early release from custody for having completed 25 years in jail.Salem, who is serving a sentence in connection with the 1993 Mumbai serial blasts, was extradited from Portugal on November 11, 2005, following a prolonged legal battle.The extradition agreement between India and Portugal stipulated that Salem could not be sentenced to death and that his prison term could not exceed 25 years.A bench comprising Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta upheld Bombay High Court’s April ruling, which had rejected his plea for immediate release, terming it “premature” and “misconceived”.A detailed order is yet to be released.Earlier in Feb, the Supreme Court refused to entertain Salem’s plea, which claimed that he was in "illegal custody" for over 10 months as he had already undergone the 25-year sentence awarded to him in the March 12, 1993, Mumbai serial bomb blasts case.
Article Summary: Salem is serving a sentence in connection with the 1993 Mumbai serial blasts. He was extradited from Portugal on November 11, 2005, following a prolonged legal battle. The extradition agreement between India and Portugal stipulated that Salem could not be sentenced to death and that his prison term could not exceed 25 years.

Article Title: 'I didn't see any benefits': Congress's P Chidambaram questions 2026 Brics, draws BJP's flak
Article Text:
Chidambaram's remarks came as authorities in the capital intensified preparations for the Brics summit.

BJP hits back at Congress

Delhi steps up preparations

NEW DELHI: Senior Congress leader and Rajya Sabha MP P Chidambaram has questioned what India has gained from recent Brics meetings, saying he has not seen any tangible benefits from the last two or three summits.With India set to host the Brics Summit 2026 in Delhi, Chidambaram said the country is part of several major international groupings but questioned whether they had delivered concrete gains for India.“I don't know how many Presidents and how many Prime Ministers are coming. I don't think the last two or three Brics summits have resulted in tangible benefits or tangible results,” Chidambaram told news agency ANI.“In fact, we are part of Brics, we are part of SCO, we are part of G20, and we are part of Quad. What benefits are we getting out of that? I can't see. In the last two or three summits, I didn't see any benefits. Earlier, the Brics Summits resulted in some tangible benefits,” he added.Reacting to Chidambaram's remarks, BJP leader Nalin Kohli said it was surprising that the Congress leader had raised such questions at a time when India was preparing to host an important international event that would bring together several heads of state and government."One is surprised to note the statement of Mr Chidambaram and the Congress Party, particularly at a time when India is hosting such an important event, the BRICS Summit, where many heads of state and heads of government will come, and there will be direct meetings also, one-on-one meetings between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and these leaders," Kohli said.Questioning the approach adopted by the Congress towards diplomacy, the BJP leader asked whether international engagement should be assessed merely in terms of immediate, transactional gains."Is diplomacy to be seen as a transaction like the Congress Party is projecting? What have I done for you? What will you do for me? Kind of an approach. What is the so-called tangible result?" he said.Kohli then questioned the Congress party's own diplomatic record from Independence until 2014."If we talk of tangible results, we can question what the Congress Party's entire approach from 1947 right up to 2014 was on diplomacy, including Sharm El Sheikh and peer projecting Pakistan as literally a victim of terror when it is the perpetrator of terror," he stated.Chidambaram's remarks came as authorities in the capital intensified preparations for the summit. Delhi Municipal Corporation Commissioner Sanjeev Khirwar and PWD Principal Secretary Sandeep Kumar inspected key areas on Wednesday, including the summit venue and locations around Bharat Mandapam.Senior officials from both departments, including deputy commissioners from the concerned zones, accompanied them during the inspection.Khirwar reviewed sanitation and civic arrangements and directed officials to coordinate closely on cleanliness and other essential services.Officials were asked to carry out intensive cleaning and maintenance along summit routes, venues, adjoining areas, markets, roads, footpaths, green belts and other sensitive locations.The inspection also covered movement corridors in southeast Delhi, including Sarai Kale Khan, Lodhi Road and Nizamuddin, as well as Saket and Sheikh Sarai in south Delhi.Authorities were directed to deploy sufficient sanitation workers, machinery and supervisory staff during the final stage of preparations.Khirwar also called for visible improvements in enforcement, animal control, vector control, beautification, lighting and branding at identified locations.India is taking over the Brics chairship for the fourth time in 2026. The chairship is being guided by the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”, with a stated focus on a people-centric and humanity-first approach.
Article Summary: Senior Congress leader and Rajya Sabha MP P Chidambaram has questioned what India has gained from recent Brics meetings. He said he has not seen any tangible benefits from the last two or three summits. India is set to host the Brics Summit 2026 in Delhi.

Article Title: 'Wonder if I should become a cockroach': Vijay Mallya cries 'injustice' over bank dues

Mentions Rs 14,131.60 crore recovery

NEW DELHI: Vijay Mallya , declared a fugitive by the government, quipped on X about "becoming a cockroach", wondering if he may have a "better life on the cockroach side" as he cried "injustice" over legal action linked to his bank dues.Mallya, who is living in London, made the remarks while responding to the legal proceedings against him and defending his position on the recovery of money owed to banks by his now-defunct Kingfisher Airlines "With all the injustices I have faced and continue to face, I wonder if I should become a cockroach. Maybe a better life on the cockroach side," he wrote on X.He cited an Enforcement Directorate (ED) affidavit that he claimed was filed before the Bombay high court and alleged that the agency had confirmed the recovery of more than Rs 14,000 crore and its transfer to banks."And may I say again, affidavit filed in court by the most feared criminal agency the Enforcement Directorate confirms that they handed over Rs 14,000 plus crores to the Banks in 2021. Forget what I say if you don’t trust me. Focus on what the Enforcement Directorate said," he alleged.Mallya also argued that repayment of bank dues should not depend on his physical presence in India."Thank you all for your mixed replies to my tweets. Love and hate go hand in hand and I respectfully accept that whilst humbly accepting your opinions.But for those who do not understand the difference between permanent residency and citizenship and for those who think that repayments are based on physical presence, please think again," he claimed.A day earlier, he had said he was legally unable to leave the UK, where he claimed to have been a permanent resident since 1992."For all who say I am a bhagoda refusing to come to India, please be aware that I have been a permanent resident of the United Kingdom since 1992 and am currently legally prohibited from leaving this country. All this started with poster boy actions by the Government of India who have been grossly unjust in my case," he said in the post on X.Mallya posted what he described as an extract from an ED affidavit filed before the Bombay high court and pointed to the figure of Rs 14,131.60 crore."Affidavit filed by the ED in the Hon’ble Bombay high court. Para 7 is the decreed debt and Para 17 shows recovered Rs 14,131.60 crore in 2021 !! 5 years on I am still referred to as a fraud who cheated the Banks," he said.He also shared a table that he claimed showed the recovery made in his case and questioned why he continued to be described as a fraudster."To all who believe in fair and proper accounting justice please see the following table. Do I still deserve the way I am berated by the media and referred to as a fraudster at the very outset of a journalist’s script ? Why not start asking when I will get my refund," he said.Mallya was among 15 people declared Fugitive Economic Offenders under the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018, according to a statement made by MoS Finance Pankaj Chaudhary in the Lok Sabha in October 2025. The list also included Nirav Modi.In February this year, the Bombay high court criticised Mallya and said he could not seek equitable relief while deliberately avoiding court proceedings. The court gave him a final opportunity to clarify whether he intended to return to India.Mallya's petition challenges the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act and his declaration as a fugitive economic offender.
Article Summary: Vijay Mallya, declared a fugitive by the government, quipped on X about "becoming a cockroach" He wondered if he may have a "better life on the cockroach side" as he cried "injustice" over legal action linked to his bank dues. He made the remarks while responding to the legal proceedings against him and defending his position on the recovery of money owed to banks.

Article Title: West Asia conflict likely hindrance to cementing Brics declaration
Article Text:
West Asia conflict likely hindrance to cementing BRICS declaration

Cannot predict outcome of declaration: Russian minister

NEW DELHI: India’s push for agreement at the BRICS summit beginning Sept 12 faces divisions among its members over the West Asia conflict.Russian officials, speaking to their country’s media, have acknowledged difficult negotiations, while Brazilian reporting has raised doubts about a strong final declaration. Yet Chinese commentary has highlighted opportunities for India’s presidency, including closer trade ties. These contrasting accounts suggest that the challenge for New Delhi is to keep economic cooperation moving while finding language that countries with conflicting security interests can accept.The Sept 12–13 summit at Bharat Mandapam will bring these differences into focus. A final declaration records the common positions that participating countries have agreed to support.Russian deputy foreign minister Sergey Ryabkov told TASS that some members were sharply critical of Tehran’s actions, making the Gulf situation Brics’ most pressing political issue. “And as of today, I cannot predict what the outcome will be,” he said about negotiations on the final document.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov acknowledged that Iran–UAE differences complicated drafting, but expressed confidence that diplomats would find acceptable wording.The disagreement concerns what members want Brics to say about the conflict. Iran’s Mehr agency reported its judiciary chief’s call at a preparatory meeting for condemnation of US–Israeli attacks. UAE agency WAM highlighted Emirati criticism of Iranian attacks on commercial shipping and demands to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.Chinese commentary has focused on India’s economic strengths. A Global Times article carried by People’s Daily praised its strengths in digital techn and medicine, while saying that bridging differences among members would test Indian diplomacy.Another Global Times commentary advocated deeper India–China trade and greater Chinese market access for Indian products. Indian reporting has highlighted New Delhi’s concerns about Chinese restrictions on critical technologies and industrial components.In Brazil, CNN Brasil reported that President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva would prioritise poll campaigning and send foreign minister Mauro Vieira. South Africa’s Business Day questioned whether expansion had weakened Brics’ unity, while broadcaster SABC highlighted Pretoria’s push for trade, industrialisation and African infra investment.For India, success would mean reaching useful agreements on specific issues while negotiating a common political message among partners whose interests do not always coincide.
Article Summary: India’s push for agreement at the BRICS summit beginning Sept 12 faces divisions among its members over the West Asia conflict. Russian officials have acknowledged difficult negotiations, while Brazilian reporting has raised doubts about a strong final declaration. Yet Chinese commentary has highlighted opportunities for India's presidency, including closer trade ties.

Article Title: J&K launches 3-year rehab scheme for drug addicts
Article Text:

SRINAGAR: J&K chief secretary Atal Dulloo Wednesday rolled out a three-year scheme to rehabilitate drug addicts under treatment at govt-run or aided de-addiction centres and institutions, prevent relapse, and aid their reintegration into society.The scheme will initially be introduced in the districts of Jammu, Srinagar, Kathua and Budgam and later extended to others, officials said.Under the scheme, a structured rehabilitation cycle will be established for drug abusers to ensure a seamless transition from “detoxification to socio-economic stabilisation” to reduce relapse rates and prevent premature exit from treatment, Dulloo said.The first six months will cover intake, assessment, treatment, stabilisation and rehabilitation planning under Phase I. The next six to 24 months will involve reintegration and livelihood activation under Phase II. The following 24-36 months will revolve around sustained monitoring and social inclusion.J&K home department will facilitate tracing and support for individuals requiring intervention. The health and medical education department will provide continuing mental health services, counselling, psychiatric care, de-addiction treatment and relapse-prevention support.The education department will aid educational reintegration, academic continuity, re-enrolment, bridge learning and access to student support services, officials said.The labour and employment department will facilitate vocational training, skill development, employment placement and entrepreneurship development. The rural development and Panchayati Raj department will support community participation, family engagement, livelihood inclusion, social support networks and local-level rehabilitation and reintegration initiatives. The social welfare department will serve as the nodal department for implementation of the policy, officials said.On April 11, 2026, J&K Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha launched a 100-day anti-drug campaign under the “Nasha Mukt Abhiyaan”, which involved large-scale awareness programmes by the civil administration and police, destruction of poppy cultivation, random urine testing of drivers and intensified crackdowns on drug networks.Over 32,500 drug abuse cases have been registered across J&K since 2022, with the highest number of patients reported from Srinagar and Jammu districts, govt data revealed. A 2022 study by Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences Kashmir estimated about 67,468 people in 10 Kashmir districts as “substance-dependent”.
Article Summary: The scheme will initially be introduced in the districts of Jammu, Srinagar, Kathua and Budgam. The first six months will cover intake, assessment, treatment, stabilisation and rehabilitation planning. The next six to 24 months will involve reintegration and livelihood activation.

Article Title: Can husband be tried for marital rape if law says not offence: Supreme Court
Article Text:
Centre should go back to drawing board if law has a problem, says SC

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Citing Article 20(1) of the Constitution which shields persons from prosecution for an act which is not an offence under existing penal laws, the Supreme Court on Wednesday asked whether a husband can be prosecuted for marital rape when the law categorically states that it is not an offence, even as it agreed with the Centre that the matter should be left for Parliament’s consideration.Article 20(1) provides that “no person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of law in force at that time…” Section 375(2) of IPC said “sexual intercourse or sexual acts by a man with his wife, the wife not being under 15 years, is not rape” (wife’s age was raised to 18 by SC in 2017), with the provision replicated in Sect 63(2) of BNS.With a bunch of petitions challenging the constitutional validity of this exception to rape, a bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said the matter posed foundational questions, especially citing the case in which a husband has challenged a Karnataka high court decision to permit his prosecution for marital rape.The hearing saw Solicitor General Tushar Mehta arguing that the issue, given its complexity, be left for the Parliament to consider.It will be absurd for courts to take upon themselves the task of determining the nature of sex — natural or unnatural — when it is best left to people, their representatives and legislature, SG Tushar Mehta said.The bench agreed. “It should always come from Parliament. If the govt feels there is a problem with the law, then it should go back to the drawing board and recast the law with approval of Parliament,” it said.During the last hearing, SC had wondered whether the court can rewrite penal laws to create a new offence.Senior advocate Karuna Nundy said that no new offence needs to be created as the offence of rape is already defined and the only question is whether it is constitutionally justified to grant immunity from it to a class of persons (husbands).
Article Summary: Supreme Court asked whether a husband can be prosecuted for marital rape when the law categorically states that it is not an offence. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta argued that the issue, given its complexity, be left for the Parliament to consider.

Indians may believe better opportunities for growth and prosperity lie offshore, yet they remain remarkably bullish about their education system, their degrees and, above all, the future of their youth.More than half of Indian respondents rate the country’s education system as good. Three-fourths believe youth will have a better life than their parents. Nearly two-thirds think even young people from lesser privileged backgrounds have a bright future. And Indians remain strikingly convinced that a university degree still has value. However, ironically, 76% of Indian respondents say young people would have better opportunities by moving abroad.For some parameters, TOI looked at the subset of India’s position among the 16 individual G20 member countries included in the 31-country Ipsos survey. China, Russia and Saudi Arabia were not surveyed. The survey covered 23,537 online adults across the 31 countries between June and July 2026, with about 1,000 respondents in India.Ipsos in its methodology has cautioned that its India sample is more urban, educated and/or affluent than the general population and should be interpreted as reflecting the views of the country’s more “connected” segment.The 31-country average is an unweighted average of country results; it is not adjusted for the population size of each country.The first question was straightforward. How do people rate the overall quality of their country’s education system? In India, 51% called it good. Among the G20 countries covered by the survey, only Australia was higher, at 53%. The 31-country average was 33%. But that 51% is a number in retreat. India was at 65% in 2025, 69% in 2024 and 55% in 2023. The 14-point fall from 2025 is the steepest year-on-year decline among countries with comparable 2025 data.The contrast with several richer economies is sharp. Britain was at 43%, the US and Brazil at 32%, Italy at 29%, Japan at 24%, while France and Germany were both at 17%. That does not mean India has a better-performing education system than advanced economies. This is a matter of perception. And on that measure, Indians appear unusually confident. Just less than before.The gap becomes even more striking when the question shifts from institutions to the people coming out of them. Asked whether young people in their country have a bright future, 72% of Indian respondents agreed. That was not merely the highest figure among the G20 countries covered. It was the highest among all 31 countries surveyed. The 31-country average was 45%.Within the surveyed G20 set, Australia and South Africa were next at 54%, followed by Mexico at 52% and Canada at 50%. France was at 22%. It is perhaps one of the strongest votes of confidence in the survey. Indians appear to have placed enormous hope in their youth to put the country on the right track and take it forward.One of the hallmarks of an aspirational society like India is the belief in accumulating wealth and opportunity across generations. People believe that the hard work of one generation will make the lives of those that follow smoother. That belief gets backed in this survey. Three-fourths of Indian respondents, 75%, believe young people today will have a better life than their parents. The 31-country average is 48%.Indians are also optimistic about people escaping the poverty trap. 64% believe young people from poorer backgrounds have a bright future, compared with a 31-country average of 40%. India is the highest among the G20 countries covered on both measures. And 69% of Indian respondents believe the education system contributes to reducing social inequalities, again the highest among the surveyed G20 countries. That figure is also below earlier readings, 72% in 2024 and 79% in 2023.Together, these numbers suggest that Indian respondents continue to see education as a vehicle for upward social mobility. That belief becomes even clearer when the survey turns to higher education. NITI Aayog ’s recent report also points to the continuing pull of degree programmes, noting that vocational pathways are often not seen as credible, growth-oriented alternatives and that degrees can become the safer choice amid limited counselling, social bias and low trust in existing skill systems. The Ipsos survey, albeit with a more urban and connected Indian sample, points in a similar direction. 75% of Indian respondents say a college or university degree is very important to succeed in life. 78% believe it helps people go further in their careers. And 70% say degrees in their country offer good value for money.On the first measure, India is the highest among the G20 countries surveyed. On both the other measures, it ranks second. The contrast with several advanced economies is large. On whether a degree is good value for money, India’s 70% compares with 38% in the US, 41% in Germany, 30% in Japan and 28% in Britain. Ipsos itself finds a strong positive relationship across countries between believing that a degree helps a career and believing that it offers value for money.Here again, the Ipsos study broadly aligns with a concern flagged in NITI Aayog’s skilling report that education and credentials do not automatically translate into the skills and pathways that the labour market demands. The Ipsos survey shows a deep-seated faith in formal education and yet a growing realisation that job-market demands are at times different from what is being taught in the classroom.Asked whether the school curriculum adequately prepares students for future careers, 67% of Indians agree, the highest share among the G20 countries covered by the survey. Even here, the direction has been downward: 74% agreed in 2024, 72% in 2025 and 67% now.Yet in another question on the greatest challenges facing young people, 36% of Indian respondents select “education and training systems not matching labour market demands”. That too is the highest among the G20 countries in the survey.India again falls on one extreme of a scatter plot for its two seemingly contradictory sets of beliefs. On one hand, 72% say young people have a bright future. On the other hand, 76% say young people would have better opportunities by moving abroad. The 31-country average on that question is 62%.Indonesia and South Africa are even more likely to say opportunities are better overseas, at 87% and 80% respectively. Italy is at 79%. Romania matches India at 76%. But none combines that level of outward-looking aspiration with India’s exceptional optimism about the future of its young.This is perhaps the central finding of the entire report for India. Respondents may be optimistic about India’s young people precisely because they believe those young people possess education and skills that give them more options, including the option of leaving. The optimism may be about the people. The doubt may be about the location of opportunity.The dichotomy in the approach of Indians extends to technology too. 78% support banning social media for children under 14, both inside and outside school. The 31-country average is 73%.Support has climbed 10 points in a year. India was at 68% in 2025 and 73% in 2024.On smartphones, 57% of Indian respondents favour a ban in schools, exactly matching the 31-country average. That is up from 50% last year and 52% in 2024. But attitudes to AI are different.Only 26% of Indian respondents say AI, including ChatGPT, should be banned in schools, compared with 39% across the 31 countries. Indian opinion on AI has moved sharply over the four editions of the survey. 39% wanted AI banned in schools in both 2025 and 2024, compared with just 16% in 2023. The 13-point drop from 2025 to 2026 is the largest year-on-year fall among countries with comparable 2025 data.Britain, the US and Poland moved in the other direction, rising to 52%, 56% and 46%, respectively.To sum up, India’s ‘connected’ population has not lost faith in education. Quite the opposite. It remains unusually convinced that education matters, degrees pay, children can surpass their parents and those from poorer homes can climb. What appears less certain is where that promise will ultimately be realised.andmay finally be different. That is the sobering realisation one can derive from this survey.
Article Summary: More than half of Indian respondents rate the country’s education system as good. Three-fourths believe youth will have a better life than their parents. Nearly two-thirds think even young people from lesser privileged backgrounds have a bright future. Indians remain strikingly convinced that a university degree still has value.

Article Title: Brics summit in Delhi on September 12-13: Agenda, schedule and other details
Article Text:
The two-day summit will bring leaders together for closed-door talks, an innovation showcase, discussions on global governance

Building resilience

The two-day BRICS summit in New Delhi, set to kick-off Saturday, will focus on strengthening cooperation in food and energy security, health, disaster resilience and critical supply chains, as member countries seek to build greater resilience amid a fragmented geopolitical environment.The summit, hosted by India under its 2026 chairship, will also cover trade, investment, connectivity and technology, while leaders are expected to exchange views on major global and regional developments.Under India's resilience pillar, leaders will discuss cooperation in areas including health, agriculture, food and energy security, disaster-risk reduction and critical supply chains. The discussions come against the backdrop of disruptions caused by geopolitical conflicts and growing concerns over the resilience of global supply networks.Strengthening intra-BRICS trade and investment, improving connectivity and expanding cooperation in high technology will also be among the key economic priorities. India has placed these areas at the centre of its broader effort to deepen cooperation among emerging economies.The summit will also focus on strengthening multilateralism and making global governance more inclusive. The first closed-door session on Saturday is titled “Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism.”Leaders will exchange views on global and regional developments and discuss areas of mutual interest, according to the Ministry of External Affairs.The main open session on Sunday is titled “Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth.” The summit will culminate with the release of the New Delhi Declaration.2:35 pm: Closed-door session for BRICS member countries on “Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism”.4:25 pm: Leaders will tour the Bharat Innovates Exhibition.5:05 pm: Leaders will assemble at Bharat Mandapam for the family photo, followed by a joint tree-planting ceremony.7:30 pm: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host a gala dinner for the leaders.9:55 am: Leaders from BRICS member countries, partner nations and outreach invitees will begin arriving.10:35 am: Official group photo.10:50 am: Open session on “Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth”.The summit will conclude with the release of the New Delhi Declaration.Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Russian President Vladimir Putin, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto are among the leaders expected to attend the summit, reported PTI.The summit comes against the backdrop of the global economy facing disruptions from the Russia-Ukraine war, the West Asia crisis, including concerns over the Strait of Hormuz, and the trade and tariff policies of the Trump administration.With the grouping operating on consensus, questions also remain over whether members will agree on a joint statement, particularly amid differences between Iran and the UAE over the West Asia crisis.BRICS originally comprised Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. The group expanded in 2024 to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, while Indonesia joined in 2025.Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam became BRICS partner countries in 2025.The grouping now has 11 member countries, representing around 49.5% of the world's population, 40% of global GDP and 26% of global trade, according to the Indian government.India assumed its fourth BRICS chairship on January 1 this year having previously chaired the grouping in 2012, 2016 and 2021.India's chairship is guided by the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”, with a stated focus on a people-centric approach rooted in the principle of “humanity first”.Under India's chairship, more than 350 meetings and high-level engagements have been held across more than 25 cities, covering the grouping's three broad pillars: political and security cooperation, economic and financial cooperation, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges.
Article Summary: Two-day BRICS summit in New Delhi will focus on food and energy security, health, disaster resilience and critical supply chains. Summit, hosted by India under its 2026 chairship, will also cover trade, investment, connectivity and technology. Leaders are expected to exchange views on major global and regional developments.

Article Title: El Nino puts India on high health-risk radar, says WHO
Article Text:
El Nino puts India on high health-risk radar, says WHO

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: With dengue cases rising in several parts of the country, a WHO assessment has flagged India among nations facing high or very high health risks as a strengthening El Nino event alters weather patterns across South Asia.El Nino is a periodic warming of surface waters in central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean that can disrupt weather patterns around the world, influencing rainfall and temperatures far beyond the Pacific.WHO's Global Public Health Situation Analysis - El Nino 2026, released on Sept 5, has identified India as being at high or very high risk, with most of South Asia expected to experience drier-than-normal conditions and above-normal heat during Aug-Oct.The warning comes at a time when vector-borne diseases are already rising in parts of the country. In Delhi, 90 dengue cases were reported in Aug, the highest monthly tally this year, taking the total to 311 by Aug 29. Malaria cases also rose from 17 in July to 53 in Aug, taking the year's tally to 119, according to Municipal Corporation of Delhi.The agency does not link current dengue or malaria cases directly to El Nino, but calls it a risk modifier, with impacts depending on local weather, vulnerability and health-system capacity.For India, heat is a key concern, with higher temperatures potentially causing heat exhaustion and heatstroke and worsening cardiovascular, respiratory, kidney and metabolic illnesses.Extreme heat may also affect maternal and newborn outcomes. Other concerns include malnutrition, food insecurity and worsening non-communicable diseases. Changes in rainfall and water availability could affect food production, while heavy rain and flooding can increase the risk of leptospirosis, particularly where sanitation and drainage are poor. WHO has also flagged the India-Nepal and India-Bhutan borders, where displacement could increase the risk of cross-border disease transmission.
Article Summary: El Nino is a periodic warming of surface waters in central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. It can disrupt weather patterns around the world, influencing rainfall and temperatures far beyond the Pacific. Most of South Asia expected to experience drier-than-normal conditions and above-normal heat during Aug-Oct.

Article Title: Pay Rs 15L to 'outstanding' officer shunted out as 'deadwood': Supreme Court
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Taking exception to Centre declaring an "outstanding" Indian Trade Service officer "dead wood" and punishing him with compulsory retirement, Supreme Court Wednesday directed all pecuniary benefits and notional promotions to him be restored and ordered govt to pay him Rs 15 lakh as compensation. S S Das was forced to retire in 2018, five years before his superannuation.A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu, which had directed Centre to place dossiers and the annual confidential record of the officer before it, found he was consistently graded as outstanding/very good from 1994 and promoted just months before the punishment. It directed govt to grant Das the honourable farewell he would have been entitled to had he not been forced to retire."The manner of decision-making in course whereof 'OUTSTANDING' gradings are completely ignored, grant of promotion is looked upon as if it were a ministerial exercise, followed by a vague and omnibus finding that it is not desirable in public interest to retain the appellant in service, discloses that the officers entrusted to take a decision were determined to ensure the appellant's ouster at any cost and invented reasons to sustain a pre-decided conclusion," the bench said, calling the exercise "sheer abuse of high offices"."Having promoted the appellant, barely a couple of months later, the superior officers in the department could not have branded him... 'dead wood' to justify weeding him out. The two actions are mutually destructive and cannot co-exist," it said.SC said the action demolished the reputation of an officer which was uncalled for. It directed that Das be called to the office by the director general of foreign trade for a farewell with full honours."It must be remembered by all and sundry that reputation is not built overnight. It is built by years of dedicated and selfless service. It comes at a great cost, often at the cost of family life and personal comfort. Such a reputation earned by sweat and toil over decades can, however, be marred by a single stroke of a pen," the bench said.SC said FR 56(j) - which gives Centre the right to prematurely retire a govt servant - should not be exercised lightly or in a casual manner. "It must be founded on material which is credible, cogent and worthy of being acted up-on, and not on mere suspicion and conjecture," it added.
Article Summary: S S Das was forced to retire in 2018, five years before his superannuation. Supreme Court ordered govt to pay him Rs 15 lakh as compensation. Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu found he was consistently graded as outstanding/very good.

Article Title: Cyber fraud worth 5,044 crore prevented: Govt
Article Text: NEW DELHI: India is increasingly stopping cyber fraud before money leaves a victim's account. A telecom-led risk system has helped banks and payment platforms prevent suspected fraudulent transactions worth Rs 5,043.7 crore in 15 months, govt said, marking a shift from tracing stolen money to intercepting payments in real time, reports Aabhas Sharma.The Financial Fraud Risk Indicator (FRI), launched by the department of telecommunications in May 2025, assigns mobile numbers medium, high or very high risk ratings. The alerts are fed directly to banks and UPI platforms, allowing them to warn customers or block risky payments.Experts said the system's biggest achievement was making fraud operations costlier.However, fraudsters could turn to SIMs obtained through fraudulent KYC or virtual numbers. An expert said criminals could also evade mobile-number risk scores by obtaining fresh or "aged" SIM cards.
Article Summary: India is increasingly stopping cyber fraud before money leaves a victim's account. Financial Fraud Risk Indicator (FRI) assigns mobile numbers medium, high or very high risk ratings. alerts are fed directly to banks and UPI platforms, allowing them to warn customers or block risky payments.

NEW DELHI: Indicating that govt is unlikely to increase ethanol blending in petrol beyond the current 20% (E20) for existing vehicles, adviser to PM Tarun Kapoor said Wednesday that allowing higher ethanol blending will have to be an option with flex-fuel vehicles.Addressing an event of sugar industry body Isma virtually, Kapoor said E20 has been very successful. “Now, our focus is on going into flex-fuel vehicles and allowing blending at a percentage which will be higher than E20, and definitely it will have to be an option for flex-fuel vehicles,” he added.He noted that several vehicle manufacturers have announced plans to roll out flex-fuel vehicles. These vehicles can run on petrol with higher ethanol blending of up to 85% and even 100% in some cases. Kapoor said there is a possibility of more such vehicles hitting the road while mentioning some petrol pumps are already making higher blends available and that this needs expansion.“But it has to go hand-in-hand with the availability of flex-fuel vehicles,” the top bureaucrat said.Dismissing criticisms against ethanol blending in petrol, Kapoor said it may be due to “misinformation or certain other motivated reasons”.He said a lot of studies and experiments have shown that E20 is good and works very well. Kapoor said there may be “a little bit of fuel efficiency”, but the decline gets compensated with higher octane. He said the issues which are being faced are generally due to “other reasons, not due to this blending”.Kapoor also said if India can also get some product which can be used in diesel, then it will be great considering that in a refinery, a large percentage of the product is diesel.“So we can’t have petrol demand going down, whereas diesel demand is going up. So, we would like to balance that; we need something to add to diesel also. And if experiments are going on on isobutanol, if that succeeds, then that would open another area where biofuels can be required in large quantities, and then that would be great for us,” he added.
Article Summary: India’s ethanol production capacity has surpassed the requirements for blending, prompting the government to explore additional uses for the surplus. Adviser to PM Tarun Kapoor said allowing higher ethanol blending will have to be an option with flex-fuel vehicles.

Article Title: India launches ORV Sagar Manthan, boosting ocean research fleet

NEW DELHI: The Government on Wednesday launched state-of-the-art ocean research vessel ORV Sagar Manthan at Rishi Bankim Shipyard in Kolkata, boosting India’s efforts towards self-reliance in oceanographic science and maritime technology.Constructed under Vertical-4 (Deep Ocean Survey and Exploration) of the government’s flagship Deep Ocean Mission (DOM) at a cost of around Rs 840 crore, the vessel is an all-weather, multidisciplinary platform. It is engineered to operate in extreme oceanic environments, including the Southern Ocean, with a projected service life of 30 years.The ORV Sagar Manthan, designed, engineered and constructed by defence public sector undertaking Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers Limited (GRSE), will gradually replace the iconic 43-year-old ORV Sagar Kanya, procured from Germany in 1983.“Today, the world knows very little about our oceans, yet they provide vital inputs about melting polar glaciers, maritime impact, and climate dynamics. Solid data collected by vessels like ORV Sagar Manthan will allow India to lead the global path in disaster prevention, take corrective environmental measures, and play a pivotal role in global ocean geopolitics,” said Union minister of earth sciences Jitendra Singh, who virtually joined the launch event.ORV Sagar Manthan will support multidisciplinary exploration along Indian Ocean mid-oceanic ridges to identify multi-metal hydrothermal sulphide mineralisation, establish environmental baselines and collect upper-air data. It integrates dynamic positioning, multibeam bathymetry, multichannel seismic systems, sub-bottom profiling, weather radar, drop keels and deployment facilities for remotely operated and autonomous underwater vehicles.
Article Summary: The vessel is an all-weather, multidisciplinary platform. It is engineered to operate in extreme oceanic environments, including the Southern Ocean. It will gradually replace the iconic 43-year-old ORV Sagar Kanya, procured from Germany in 1983.

Article Title: Centre clears separate engineering cadre for Delhi PWD

Centre clears separate engineering cadre for Delhi PWD

NEW DELHI: The Centre has approved the Delhi government's proposal to create a separate engineering cadre for the Public Works Department (PWD), a move expected to give the capital greater control over its engineering workforce and help speed up infrastructure projects.Under the decision, 3,214 sanctioned engineering posts across 36 categories in Delhi PWD will be separated from the Central Public Works Department (CPWD) cadre and brought under an independent Delhi PWD Engineering Cadre.Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta welcomed the approval, describing it as a historic step towards making Delhi a developed, safe and world-class capital.The Delhi government said the separate cadre is intended to address a long-standing administrative issue and make the PWD's engineering system more responsive to the capital's specific requirements. The proposal had earlier been approved by the Delhi Cabinet under Gupta's leadership.The issue has remained pending for nearly 30 years. Until now, Delhi PWD's engineering services were largely dependent on the CPWD cadre, with appointments to its sanctioned posts being made through the Central government's system.According to the Delhi government, this arrangement could sometimes make it difficult to take decisions quickly in line with Delhi's own development and administrative requirements.Gupta said Delhi's infrastructure needs are distinct because of the scale and pace of development in the national capital. The city requires continuous construction and maintenance of roads, bridges, government buildings, offices and other public infrastructure.With the creation of a separate cadre, the Delhi government will have greater control over its engineering workforce. It will be able to manage issues such as filling vacancies, ensuring the availability of engineers, monitoring projects and deploying officials according to the requirements of different works.The government also expects the new arrangement to help build an engineering workforce more familiar with Delhi's local infrastructure challenges and development priorities.The move comes as the government prepares to undertake several major construction and development projects. These include a new secretariat and mini-secretariats in all 11 districts, besides work related to mandis, sports grounds and other public facilities.Roads, bridges and other infrastructure projects will also require sustained engineering support across the capital.The government said the reform is not limited to changing the administrative structure of engineering posts. It is also intended to improve accountability and transparency in the execution of public works.Gupta said that under the earlier system, instances involving deficiencies or irregularities in construction projects could sometimes make it difficult to fix responsibility, particularly when the concerned officer was transferred.A separate Delhi PWD cadre, the government said, would allow the responsibilities of engineering officials and the monitoring of their work to be linked more closely with the Delhi government's administrative system.The Centre's approval now provides the formal basis for Delhi PWD to establish an independent engineering cadre. The government believes the move will make the department more self-reliant and help ensure greater continuity in the planning, execution and supervision of infrastructure projects.For a rapidly developing capital facing growing demands on its roads, public buildings and other infrastructure, the decision marks a significant administrative change that could shape how Delhi's public works are planned and delivered in the years ahead.
Article Summary: The Centre has approved the Delhi government's proposal to create a separate engineering cadre for the Public Works Department. The move is expected to give the capital greater control over its engineering workforce and help speed up infrastructure projects. Until now, Delhi PWD's engineering services were largely dependent on the CPWD cadre.

NEW DELHI: Defence minister Rajnath Singh on Wednesday met Sri Lankan President Anura Kumara Dissanayake in Colombo and discussed the multi-faceted partnership between the two countries, including cooperation to ensure the safety, security, peace and prosperity of the region.Singh arrived in Sri Lanka on Tuesday for a three-day visit. His visit is the first by an Indian defence minister to the island nation in 38 years.Singh conveyed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's greetings to Dissanayake and congratulated him on the completion of two years of his government. He also underlined the deep friendship between the people of India and Sri Lanka, based on their historical and civilisational links.“The two sides reaffirmed that as civilisational twins, close neighbours and maritime partners, India and Sri Lanka would continue to work together for their development and welfare of the people while working jointly to ensure the safety, security, peace and prosperity of the region,” the ministry of defence said.Singh described the meeting as “warm and extremely productive” in a post on X.Dissanayake recalled his interactions with Prime Minister Modi and reiterated that Sri Lanka would never allow its territory to be used for activities inimical to India's security interests, the ministry of defence said.The Sri Lankan president also expressed gratitude for India's relief assistance under Operation Sagar Bandhu during Cyclone Ditwah and the comprehensive rehabilitation package extended by New Delhi for reconstruction and rehabilitation.Singh said India considered assistance to Sri Lanka a responsibility rather than a favour.“As a closest friend and neighbour of Sri Lanka, India considered it not a favour, but a responsibility to assist as the first responder and would continue to do so in the future as well,” he said.Both leaders also virtually inaugurated three Bailey Bridges constructed by Indian defence forces.India and Sri Lanka exchanged memorandums of understanding on the upgradation of L70 guns for the Sri Lankan Air Force and cooperation between the National Cadet Corps (NCC) and National Defence Colleges (NDC) of both countries.The MoU on the upgradation of six L70 guns for the Sri Lankan Air Force falls under an Indian government grant. The programme provides an opportunity for NCC cadets from multiple countries to travel to New Delhi each year and participate in NCC events.Singh is leading a high-level delegation comprising senior officials from the ministries of defence and external affairs.Singh's visit also included an interaction with the Indian diaspora in Colombo, where he said India would stand firmly with Sri Lanka during times of crisis.“The relationship between India and Sri Lanka is based on shared history, culture, and faith. We stand with Sri Lanka through thick and thin and are committed to the peace, prosperity, and development of both countries,” Singh said, according to news agency ANI.Sri Lanka's leader of opposition Sajith Premadasa also praised India's support for the island nation after meeting Singh, describing India as a “very close partner” and the bilateral relationship as “very special”.“My meeting with Rajnath Singh was very constructive, very progressive. We have a very strong relationship with India. It is a special relationship. We are very close partners,” Premadasa said.He highlighted India's role as a first responder during Sri Lanka's economic crisis, the Covid-19 pandemic and Cyclone Ditwah.“India has always been the first responder. And Prime Minister Modi has always walked the talk. India has been the first responder in supporting Sri Lanka during Ditwah, during times of bankruptcy, and during the Corona health hazard,” Premadasa said.Premadasa said Colombo wanted to further deepen ties with India while respecting the sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence of both countries.

Article Title: Strategic Autonomy in motion as India hosts 18th BRICS Summit
Article Text:
This would be the 18th summit of the grouping. (Photo: ANI)

India for BRICS

Key Challenges for India

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India will host the annual BRICS summit on September 12-13 at Bharat Mandapam, returning to the venue where it held the G20 summit in 2023. That gathering is remembered for the inclusion of the African Union in G20, marking a major step in efforts to bridge the gap between the Western-led global order and the emerging Global South. At BRICS, India will look to leverage that momentum, working with major emerging economies to demand structural reforms of global governance institutions dominated by the West.This would be the 18th summit of the grouping that brings together 11 major emerging and developing economies – Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Ethiopia, UAE, Indonesia, Iran, Egypt and Saudi Arabia – along with 10 other partner countries. Together, BRICS nations account for 49 percent of world population, 40 percent of global GDP and 26 percent of international trade.The last time India hosted an in-person BRICS summit was in 2016 in Goa. This year also marks 2 decades of formalisation of the bloc for cooperation on issues related to global economic and political governance. The theme of India's 2026 chairship is Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability, drawing inspiration from PM Narendra Modi's 'humanity first' and people-centric approach to BRICS.This will also be the first summit to see in-person participation by Russian President Vladimir Putin since the start of the Ukraine war. Chinese President Xi Jinping is also visiting India for the first time in 7 years to participate in the summit.Under its chairship, India has so far held over 350 meetings - 25 at the ministerial level including the foreign ministers and national security advisers’ engagements. The ministerial meetings have so far resulted in key outcomes and initiatives spanning agriculture, health, energy, environment, disaster management and also trade, reaffirming commitment to a fair, inclusive and transparent multilateral trading system with WTO at its core.Despite the political fragmentation and economic imbalances associated with the grouping, BRICS remains important for India for multiple reasons, especially in an increasingly uncertain world. For one, it lends India a platform to practice its strategic autonomy and multi-alignment policy, not allowing any one single bloc to acquire excessive leverage over it. That it can simultaneously expand its strategic and technology ties with the West and also work with Quad for a free and open Indo-Pacific reinforces an independent foreign policy. For India, as external affairs minister S Jaishankar has said, BRICS is an embodiment of a multipolar world. India is not giving up on its Western partnerships, only hedging against uncertainty whether from US unpredictability or Chinese ascendancy.BRICS also allows India to showcase its Global South leadership credentials, as it works with other major emerging markets to push for reforms of global institutions like the UNSC, IMF and World Bank that are not representative of the developing world. Support for UNSC reforms is important, although it still falls short of an explicit endorsement of India's permanent membership bid, mainly because of China's presence.India's approach to BRICS is also guided by its complex ties with China. Turning away would mean allowing China to single-handedly shape the agenda of the developing world. BRICS is consensus driven and even for Washington and other Western capitals, India's moderating influence should be of significance as it prevents the bloc from turning into an anti-West platform.There's focus as well on expanding financial architecture as no government would like its trade to be held hostage by instruments it can't control. As Jaishankar has underlined, institutions such as the New Development Bank and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement demonstrate the group's ability to create credible alternatives. For India, these are not initiatives targeted at any currency. In any case, India has officially said it's against de-dollarisation or any attempt to target the US currency. It has also ruled out any proposal for a common BRICS currency.BRICS provides India with markets, along with trade diversification, de-risking and supply-chain opportunities. According to a commerce ministry press release, intra-BRICS merchandise trade reached approximately $1.17 trillion in 2024. India exported an estimated $82 billion in goods to BRICS members in FY2025–26, alongside approximately $31.3 billion in services exports in 2024. BRICS membership deepens India’s trade relationships with Russia (energy), Brazil (agriculture/commodities), Gulf and African countries, diversifying away from overreliance on any single partner.The first of course is to forge a consensus on West Asia that would enable a joint BRICS declaration, a task complicated by the presence of the UAE and Iran in the group. India would not like the event to end with a Chair's Statement, like what happened with the foreign ministers' meeting, knowing well that no BRICS summit has concluded without a comprehensive joint declaration. Foreign secretary Vikram Misri said last week India has received cooperation from all members and the government is working to arrive eventually at a constructive outcome that benefits all BRICS stakeholders. India will focus on drafting a resolution rooted in the UN Charter, dialogue and diplomacy, freedom of navigation and civilian protection, while looking to ringfence economic agreements from contentious political issues by acknowledging respective national positions.Balancing relations with the US is another key concern for India, which is hosting the summit fresh off a tariff firestorm with Washington. US President Donald Trump sees the grouping itself as an assault on the US currency and has threatened to impose 100 percent tariffs on BRICS nations if they work to replace the US dollar. India backs legitimate local-currency settlement, while maintaining it is against any common BRICS currency or China-centered replacement mechanism. As it walks the diplomatic tightrope, India must steer initiatives like the integration of central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) but without appearing to endorse any anti-dollar bloc.Another challenge for India is to prevent China's predominance without destabilising its bilateral relations with Beijing. For all the talk about BRICS' combined power, China enjoys a vastly asymmetrical influence with its trade, investment, manufacturing and critical mineral leverage. Wary of China's efforts to advance its own economic interests, India has not endorsed SCO’s 2030 economic roadmap and it must find a way to work with China in BRICS on shared objectives but without allowing the forum to be co-opted as a Chinese economic or geopolitical platform.This also intersects with the challenge of ensuring that an expanded grouping remains governable and cohesive, especially with countries like Pakistan and Bangladesh pursuing membership with support from Beijing. True multipolarity and consensus-driven equality within the organisation are key imperatives for India.As Jaishankar said while announcing India's summit agenda, BRICS must transition now from a forum for discussions to a platform for delivery. In that spirit, India seems focused on delivering an outcome-oriented summit with key deliverables like a unanimous BRICS declaration, logistics supply-chain cooperation framework, incubator/ startup network, development finance, cross-border payment and continued support for Indian priorities like UNSC reforms and counterterrorism.To conclude, inclusion of the African Union was not the only major takeaway from the G20 summit in 2023. Perhaps more dramatic was the last-minute consensus on Ukraine through a compromise language crafted by India, allowing a G20 declaration. India can take confidence from that diplomatic triumph, heading into another tough but potentially rewarding global summit.
Article Summary: India will host the annual BRICS summit on September 12-13 at Bharat Mandapam, returning to the venue where it held the G20 summit in 2023. This would be the 18th summit of the grouping that brings together 11 major emerging and developing economies – Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Ethiopia, UAE, Indonesia, Iran, Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

Article Title: Why Vijay's gold ring scheme may miss its September 15 launch
Article Text:
Under Vijay's gold ring scheme, every newborn delivered at a government health facility will receive a one-gram gold ring. At the current gold rate, the ring is worth around Rs 13,600.

What is the gold ring scheme?
